passages.t: Fallen cedars, and a flock marked for slaughter
passages.happening:
A short lament opens the chapter. Lebanon is to open its doors so that fire may consume its cedars; the cypress and the oaks of Bashan are to wail, for the great trees are ruined (verses 1-2). Listen to the wailing of the shepherds, whose glory is in ruins, and the roaring of young lions, for the thickets of the Jordan are destroyed (verse 3).

Then the LORD tells the prophet, ‘Pasture the flock marked for slaughter’ (verse 4). Those who buy them kill them without remorse, and those who sell them thank God that they are rich, and their own shepherds have no pity on them (verse 5). God will no longer pity the people of the land, but will hand each one over to his neighbor and his king (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The cedars of Lebanon and the oaks of Bashan were the proudest trees of the region, pictures of the powerful brought down. The shepherds are rulers; the lions' thickets along the Jordan are wrecked.

In verses 4 to 17 the prophet performs a sign-act, playing the part of a shepherd, as Jeremiah and Ezekiel performed theirs. The flock marked for slaughter is the people, exploited by those who buy and sell them and abandoned by their own leaders. The traders even thank God for the profit they make from the flock.

This chapter is among the hardest in the book. Which shepherds are meant is not said, and interpreters differ.
passages.later: Ezekiel condemned the shepherds who fed themselves and not the flock (Ezekiel 34:2-3). Jeremiah also spoke of a flock led astray by its shepherds (Jeremiah 50:6).
passages.asks: The traders thanked God for the profit they made from the flock. Ask whether you have ever called it God's goodness when you gained at someone else's expense. And ask who in your care might be treated as a flock marked for slaughter.

passages.t: Two staffs, thirty pieces of silver, and a worthless shepherd
passages.happening:
The prophet pastures the flock, especially the afflicted. He takes two staffs, one called Favor and the other Union (verse 7). In one month he removes three shepherds, but he grows weary of the flock, and they detest him (verse 8). He gives them up (verse 9) and breaks the staff called Favor, ending the covenant (verse 10). The afflicted who were watching know it is the word of the LORD (verse 11).

He asks for his wages, if it seems right to them. ‘So they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver’ (verse 12). The LORD tells him to throw it to the potter, ‘this magnificent price at which they valued me’ (verse 13). He throws the silver to the potter in the house of the LORD, and breaks his second staff, Union, ending the brotherhood between Judah and Israel (verse 14).

Then the LORD tells him to take up the equipment of a foolish shepherd, for God will raise up a shepherd who will not care for the lost or heal the broken (verses 15-16). Woe to the worthless shepherd who deserts the flock (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
A shepherd carried a staff, and the prophet carries two, whose names mean grace and unity. Breaking them acts out the end of God's favor and the end of the bond between the two kingdoms.

Thirty pieces of silver was the price the law set for a slave gored by an ox. To pay the shepherd that sum was an insult, which is why God calls it a magnificent price, with bitter irony. Throwing it to the potter in the house of the LORD may mean the temple treasury, or the potter who worked for the temple; the meaning is uncertain.

The worthless shepherd who follows is the opposite of the good one: he does not seek the lost or heal the broken. The chapter ends with a woe on him.
passages.later: The law set the price for a slave at ‘thirty shekels of silver’ (Exodus 21:32). Matthew says the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas and used to buy a potter's field fulfilled what was spoken, ‘They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price set on Him by the people of Israel’ (Matthew 27:9).
passages.hard:
Why does Matthew attribute a quotation from Zechariah to Jeremiah?

Matthew introduces the fulfillment with the words spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, but the thirty pieces of silver and the throwing of money to the potter come from Zechariah 11. Several explanations are offered. Many scholars point out that Matthew's quotation is a composite: it takes its wording chiefly from Zechariah but its themes of a potter, a field bought and a place of burial from Jeremiah, and Matthew names the more prominent prophet, as Mark 1:2-3 names Isaiah for a quotation that blends Malachi and Isaiah. Others suggest that Jeremiah stood first in some ancient arrangements of the prophets, so that his name could stand for the collection. These notes leave the explanations as they stand.
passages.asks: The people valued the shepherd at the price of a slave. Ask what value you have put on God's care for you. And ask what kind of shepherd you are to those who look to you.
